name: Resume design
routing_text: How should a software engineer or data scientist write their resume? Bullet points, professional summary, page length, formatting and layout, ATS keyword matching, quantified impact and metrics, tailoring a CV to one job description, and what a recruiter looks for in the seconds they spend skimming it.
blurb: What a technical resume has to do on the page before anyone reads it closely.

notes: deep-research one-shot control: the same plan taken to 10 probes in a single round, no critic

rubrics.criterion: Keep the resume to one page.
rubrics.check: Count the pages in the submitted PDF or printout; fail if it exceeds one page.
rubrics.why: Recruiters spend only seconds per resume, and extra pages add reading that slows them and dilutes what matters.

rubrics.criterion: Write every experience bullet as a full sentence that states what you did, how you did it, and the result.
rubrics.check: For each bullet under Experience, identify an action verb, a method or context, and an outcome; fail any bullet that is a generic duty with no result, such as "handled various operational duties over five years."
rubrics.why: Vague, outcome-free bullet points make you look risky; full sentences with results show the manager you have already done the job.

rubrics.why: Hiring managers decide in seconds, and the summary exists to save the recruiter time; a resume that doesn't match the job description is useless.

rubrics.criterion: Back up every claim in the summary and experience bullets with a concrete fact: a number, a percentage, a dollar amount, or a specific accomplishment from a previous role.

rubrics.why: Concrete results are what make a reader think you can repeat that win for them; without them there is no reason to believe you can do the job well.

rubrics.why: Numbers make the candidate seem more educated and invested, and recruiters say they love seeing measurable results.

rubrics.criterion: Open with a professional summary that names the target role, states your experience level, and brags about a specific accomplishment by the second sentence.
rubrics.check: Read the first section; fail if it is only an objective statement, if the role title is not matched, if experience years/environments are absent, or if the first two sentences contain no concrete accomplishment.
rubrics.why: Recruiters already know your objective; they need to know what you can do for them and why they should hire you, and mirroring the job title in the summary also improves ATS scoring.

rubrics.criterion: Give the last 5-7 years of experience the most space; compress older roles to at most two or three relevant bullet points.
rubrics.check: For every role that ended more than seven years ago, count the bullet points; fail if any such role has more than three bullet points or is given as much space as recent experience.
rubrics.why: A resume that gives equal weight to old and recent work buries what is most relevant, and recruiters need sharp signals rather than a timeline.

rubrics.why: Recruiters and ATS systems skip resumes they cannot parse, so fancy formatting sends yours to the rejection pile before the content is read.
